title: Bundles: when the package costs more
description: Bundles promise simplicity and savings. Sometimes they deliver both — and sometimes they charge you for things you never use.

body.heading: Unbundle on paper
paragraphs: Take any bundle — broadband with TV and phone, software suites, travel packages — and price the parts you would actually buy, separately. Compare that total with the bundle price. The difference is what the unused parts cost you.

Suppose a bundle is $70 a month, but the broadband alone is $40 and the rest is channels and features you would never buy separately. You are not saving on a $90 package; you are spending $30 a month — $360 a year — on decoration.

body.heading: When bundles genuinely win
paragraphs: Bundles can be excellent value when you truly use most of the parts, when one bill replaces genuine hassle, or when the combined price undercuts even your cherry-picked parts. Some combinations also include perks — shared storage, family accounts — that are awkward to assemble alone.
The test is usage, not arithmetic alone. List the parts, mark the ones used monthly, and let that honest list decide.

body.heading: Renegotiate at renewal
paragraphs: Bundle prices creep at renewal, counting on inertia. A month before renewal, repeat the unbundling exercise and phone with your figures. Providers often find a better price for customers who have clearly done the maths.

If the provider will not move, that is useful information too: you can switch with a clear list of exactly which parts you need, instead of shopping for a vague replacement and ending up with another oversized package.

takeaway: Price the parts you would actually use before accepting any bundle — and repeat the exercise at every renewal, when the quiet price rises happen.
